decks.title: Heat and Energy — Part 1: Heat, temperature and the anomalous expansion of water
goals: Distinguish heat from temperature and convert between the calorie and the joule
Describe the anomalous expansion of water and read its volume-temperature and density-temperature graphs
Describe Hope’s experiment and explain how a pond freezes and why pipes burst in winter

slides.heading: Hot, warm or cold: what is heat?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — heat is energy; temperature tells us how hot a body is. Water behaves oddly near freezing.

visual.alt: Flow from a hot body to a cold body, with heat flowing between them

slides.narration: A hot cup of tea cools down and a cold drink warms up. In both cases something flows between the drink and the room. That something is heat, and this chapter also shows why a frozen pond keeps fish alive.

slides.heading: Heat and temperature
slides.body_md: **Heat** is a form of **energy**. It flows from a body at a **higher temperature** to one at a **lower temperature**. **Temperature** tells us **how hot or cold** a body is; it decides the **direction** in which heat flows.

rows: Energy that flows because of a temperature difference
Degree of hotness of a body

visual.alt: Table comparing heat and temperature by meaning, unit, instrument and dependence on mass

slides.narration: Heat is energy on the move. Temperature is not energy at all; it is a measure of how hot something is. Heat always flows from the hotter body to the colder one, until their temperatures become equal.

slides.heading: Quick check: which way does heat flow?
slides.body_md: Think about the temperatures, not the sizes, of the two blocks.

visual.alt: Table of the temperatures of two blocks placed in contact

slides.narration: Two metal blocks, one hot and one cooler, are placed in contact. In which direction does heat flow?

slides.heading: Units of heat: joule and calorie
slides.body_md: The SI unit of heat is the **joule (J)**. The older unit, the **calorie (cal)**, is the heat needed to raise the temperature of **1 g of water by 1 °C**. **1 cal = 4.186 J**, and 1 kilocalorie (kcal) = 1000 cal.

visual.alt: Table of the joule, the calorie and the kilocalorie

slides.narration: The joule is the unit we use in science. The calorie comes from heating water: it is the heat that warms one gram of water by one degree Celsius. One calorie is about four point two joules.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: heat in calories and joules
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 300 g of water by 20 °C? Give the answer in cal and in J. (1 cal = 4.186 J)

**Step 1.** 1 cal warms 1 g by 1 °C, so heat $= 300 \times 20 = 6000$ cal.

**Step 2.** $6000 \times 4.186 = 25116$ J.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the heat in calories and in joules

slides.narration: Each gram needs one calorie for each degree. Multiply the mass by the rise in temperature to get the heat in calories. Then multiply by four point one eight six to change calories into joules.

slides.heading: Quick check: calories to joules
slides.body_md: Multiply the number of calories by 4.186.

visual.alt: Table of the heat supplied and the conversion factor

slides.narration: Four hundred calories of heat are supplied to a body. How many joules is this?

slides.heading: Most liquids expand on heating; water does not always
slides.body_md: Most liquids **expand** when heated and **contract** when cooled. Water is an exception between **0 °C and 4 °C**: when heated from 0 °C it **contracts** until 4 °C, and above 4 °C it **expands**. This is the **anomalous expansion of water**.

visual.alt: Table of how the volume and density of water change on heating in different temperature ranges

slides.narration: Warm a liquid and it normally swells. Water follows this rule above four degrees Celsius. Between zero and four degrees it does the opposite: it shrinks when heated. At four degrees its volume is smallest and its density is greatest.

slides.heading: Density against temperature
slides.body_md: The graph is drawn from measured values. Between **0 °C and 4 °C** the density **rises** and reaches its maximum, about **1000 kg m⁻³**, at **4 °C**; above 4 °C it **falls** again. The vertical scale is stretched, so the change looks bigger than it is.

slides.narration: In Hope’s experiment a tall jar of water is cooled in the middle by a freezing mixture. One thermometer reads the water near the top and the other reads the water near the bottom. Both readings are noted every few minutes.

slides.heading: Hope’s experiment: the readings
slides.body_md: The **lower thermometer** falls first and **stops at 4 °C**. Then the **upper thermometer** begins to fall and finally reaches **0 °C**. Water cooled in the middle is **denser**, so it sinks, until it reaches 4 °C, the greatest density. Colder water is **lighter** and stays on top.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: water freezing in a pipe
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A closed pipe holds 1000 cm³ of water. It freezes completely. Find the volume of the ice and the increase in volume. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; of ice 900 kg m⁻³)

**Step 1.** Mass of water $= 1000 \times 1 = 1000$ g. The mass stays the same when it freezes.

**Step 2.** Volume of ice $= \dfrac{1000}{0.9} = 1111.1$ cm³, so the increase is $1111.1 - 1000 = 111.1$ cm³.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the volume of the ice and the increase in volume

slides.narration: Freezing does not change the mass. Divide that mass by the smaller density of ice to find the larger volume. The extra space the ice needs pushes hard on the pipe, and a closed pipe can crack.

slides.heading: Why pipes burst and bottles crack
slides.body_md: Water **expands when it freezes**: ice takes up about **one-ninth more volume** than the water it came from. In a **closed pipe or sealed bottle** the ice has no room, so it exerts a very large force and the container **cracks**. That is why a full bottle should not be left in a freezer.

rows: Water pipe in a freezing night
Ice needs more space than water

visual.alt: Table of three situations in which expanding ice breaks the container

slides.narration: When water turns to ice it takes up more space. If the pipe or bottle is full and closed, the ice pushes outwards with a huge force. The container cracks. The same thing slowly widens cracks in rocks on cold mountains.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter to a colder body; temperature tells how hot a body is.
SI unit of heat: joule. 1 cal = 4.186 J; 1 kcal = 1000 cal.
Water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands above 4 °C: its density is maximum and its volume minimum at 4 °C.
Hope’s experiment: the lower thermometer stops at 4 °C, the upper falls to 0 °C. Ponds freeze from the top; the bottom stays at 4 °C. Closed pipes burst because ice occupies more volume.

visual.alt: Summary table of the calorie, the temperature of maximum density and the bottom of a frozen pond

slides.narration: To sum up Part one. Heat is energy and flows from hot to cold. One calorie is four point one eight six joules. Water is densest at four degrees Celsius, which explains Hope’s experiment, frozen ponds and burst pipes.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1

Write 1 cal = 4.186 J and show the multiplication in conversions.
Label the 4 °C on both graphs: the density graph has a peak, the volume graph a dip.

slides.heading: Why is the Earth warm enough for life?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a blanket of gases keeps the Earth warm; adding more makes it too warm. Useful energy also gets used up as heat.

visual.alt: Flow from sunlight reaching the ground to the ground giving out infrared and gases trapping some of it

slides.narration: Without its atmosphere the Earth would be far too cold for life. Certain gases act like a blanket. This part explains how the blanket works, what happens when it grows thicker, and why energy loses its usefulness.

slides.heading: The greenhouse effect
slides.body_md: **Sunlight** passes through the atmosphere and **warms the ground**. The warm ground gives out **infrared** radiation. **Greenhouse gases** absorb part of it and send some back to the ground, so the lower atmosphere stays **warmer than it would otherwise be**. This is the **greenhouse effect**.

slides.narration: Sunlight easily passes through the air and warms the ground. The ground gives out heat as infrared waves. Greenhouse gases absorb some of these waves and send part of that energy back down, keeping the surface warm.

slides.heading: Greenhouse gases
slides.body_md: The main **greenhouse gases** are **carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide** and the **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**. Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air, are **not** greenhouse gases.

rows: Paddy fields, cattle and rubbish dumps

visual.alt: Table of five greenhouse gases and a common source of each

slides.narration: Carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide and the chlorofluorocarbons all trap heat. Most of the air, nitrogen and oxygen, does not. Burning fuels, farming and rubbish all add greenhouse gases to the air.

slides.heading: Quick check: which gases trap heat?
slides.body_md: Recall which gases absorb infrared radiation.

visual.alt: Table of the shares of three gases in dry air

slides.narration: Some gases in the air absorb heat radiated by the Earth. Which pair of gases does this?

slides.heading: The natural greenhouse effect is useful
slides.body_md: Without the natural greenhouse effect the average temperature of the Earth’s surface would be about **−18 °C**, so oceans would freeze. With it, the average is about **15 °C**, which suits life. The trouble starts when **extra** greenhouse gases are added.

visual.alt: Table of the Earth’s average surface temperature without and with the natural greenhouse effect

slides.narration: The natural greenhouse effect is helpful. It raises the average temperature of the Earth’s surface from about eighteen degrees below zero to about fifteen degrees above. The danger comes from adding extra greenhouse gases.

slides.heading: Global warming: causes
slides.body_md: **Global warming** is the **rise in the average temperature of the Earth** caused by **extra greenhouse gases** added by human activity. **Causes:** burning **fossil fuels**, **cutting down forests** (fewer trees to absorb carbon dioxide), **farming and livestock**, and rubbish dumps. As of 2026, carbon dioxide in the air is above 420 parts per million, well above the level before industry.

visual.alt: Table of four human activities and the effect of each on greenhouse gases

slides.narration: Burning fuels, clearing forests, keeping cattle and growing paddy all add greenhouse gases or remove the trees that soak up carbon dioxide. As a result, the average temperature of the Earth has been rising.

slides.heading: Global warming: impact on life
slides.body_md: Rising temperatures **melt glaciers and polar ice**, which raises the **sea level** and floods coastal land. Other effects: **heat waves**, **droughts** and heavy rain, **harm to crops**, **bleaching of coral reefs** and loss of homes of animals. As of 2026, the Earth’s average temperature is roughly 1.1 to 1.3 °C above the level of the late 1800s.

rows: Floods in some places, droughts in others

visual.alt: Table of four effects of global warming and their results

slides.narration: A warmer Earth melts ice, so the sea rises and floods low coasts. It also brings heat waves, droughts, damaged crops and bleached coral reefs. Plants, animals and people all feel the change.

slides.heading: Quick check: a result of global warming
slides.body_md: Think about what happens to ice when the Earth warms.

visual.alt: Table linking more greenhouse gases to a higher average temperature

slides.narration: Which of these is a likely result of global warming?

slides.heading: What can we do?
slides.body_md: Burn **less fossil fuel**: use **solar, wind and hydro power**, save electricity, use **public transport** or cycle. **Plant trees** and protect forests. **Reduce, reuse and recycle** waste so that less rubbish rots in dumps. Everyone can help by switching off unused lights and fans.

rows: No carbon dioxide from burning fuel

visual.alt: Table of four actions that reduce global warming and why each helps

slides.narration: Using clean power, saving electricity, travelling together, planting trees and cutting waste all reduce the greenhouse gases we add. Small daily habits matter when millions of people share them.

slides.heading: Energy changes form and loses usefulness
slides.body_md: Energy is never destroyed, but in every change some of it turns into **heat that spreads into the surroundings** and cannot be fully collected for use again. The energy is still there but is **less useful**. This is **energy degradation**.

nodes.label: Heat and sound to the surroundings

visual.alt: Flow from the energy of the fuel through an engine to useful motion and heat and sound spread into the surroundings

slides.narration: Fuel stored in a car holds useful energy. The engine changes it into motion, but also into heat and sound that spread into the air. That spread-out heat cannot be gathered again. The energy has been degraded.

slides.heading: Seeing degradation: a band diagram
slides.body_md: The width of each band is **in proportion to the energy**. Of 20000 J from the fuel, 5000 J becomes useful motion and 15000 J becomes **heat spread into the surroundings**. The total is the same: **energy is conserved**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a car engine

sections.heading: 1. Heat and temperature; the joule and the calorie
sections.body_md:
**Heat** is a form of **energy** that flows from a body at a higher temperature to one at a lower temperature. **Temperature** is the **degree of hotness** of a body; it decides the direction of the flow of heat. Two bodies at the same temperature do not exchange heat. A lake and a cup of water at the same temperature are equally hot, but the lake holds far more heat because it has far more mass.

- **SI unit of heat:** joule (J). **Calorie (cal):** the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C. **1 cal = 4.186 J**. 1 kilocalorie (kcal) $= 1000$ cal $= 4186$ J; the "Calorie" on a food label is the kilocalorie.
- **SI unit of temperature:** kelvin (K); in daily life, degree Celsius (°C). A thermometer measures temperature.
- By the definition of the calorie, heating $m$ grams of water through $\Delta t$ °C needs $m \times \Delta t$ cal (if no heat is lost). Heat capacities and specific heat are taken up in Class X and are not needed here.

sections.heading: 2. Anomalous expansion of water
sections.body_md:
Most liquids expand when heated. **Water between 0 °C and 4 °C is an exception:** its volume **decreases** when it is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, and increases only above 4 °C. This is the **anomalous expansion of water**.

- **At 4 °C** a given mass of water has its **minimum volume** and its **maximum density** (about 1000 kg m⁻³; more exactly 999.97 kg m⁻³).
- **Graphs, 0 °C to 10 °C:** the **volume-temperature** graph is a **dip** with its lowest point at 4 °C; the **density-temperature** graph is a **hump** with its highest point at 4 °C. They are mirror images because density = mass ÷ volume. For 1 kg of water the volume is about 1000.16 cm³ at 0 °C, 1000.03 cm³ at 4 °C and 1000.3 cm³ at 10 °C. The changes are very small, so the vertical scale of the graphs is stretched.
- Water at 0 °C is **less dense than water at 4 °C**, and **ice is less dense than water**, so ice floats.
- The tabulated values differ slightly between books (4 °C is the rounded value of 3.98 °C).

sections.heading: 3. Hope’s experiment and the consequences of anomalous expansion
sections.body_md:
**Hope’s experiment** demonstrates that water has its greatest density at 4 °C. A **tall jar of water** has a **trough of freezing mixture** (ice and salt) around its **middle**; one thermometer is placed in the water **above** the trough and one **below** it.

- The water in the middle cools, becomes denser and **sinks**, so the **lower thermometer falls first**; it stops at **4 °C**.
- Water that is colder than 4 °C is **less dense** and stays above, so the **upper thermometer falls later** and finally reaches **0 °C**, when ice forms.

**Consequences**
- **Ponds and lakes in cold regions:** the top layer cools to 0 °C and freezes; ice floats and, being a poor conductor of heat, protects the water below. The water at the bottom stays at about 4 °C, so **fish and plants survive**.
- **Pipes and bottles:** water **expands on freezing** (ice has about 11% more volume than the water it came from), so water in a closed pipe, sealed bottle or rock crack can **burst or crack** it.

key_terms.definition_md: An experiment with a tall jar of water cooled in the middle, which shows that water is densest at 4 °C.

sections.heading: 4. Greenhouse effect and global warming
sections.body_md:
**Greenhouse effect:** sunlight (mainly visible light) passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground. The ground gives out **infrared** radiation. **Greenhouse gases** absorb part of it and **send some back** towards the ground, so the lower atmosphere is warmer than it would otherwise be. **Main greenhouse gases:** carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide and the chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs); nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.

- The **natural** greenhouse effect is **useful**: without it the average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.
- **Global warming** is the **rise in the average temperature of the Earth** caused by **extra** greenhouse gases added by human activities: burning fossil fuels, deforestation, farming and livestock, rubbish dumps.
- **Impact:** melting of glaciers and polar ice and **rise in sea level**, heat waves, droughts and floods, damage to crops, bleaching of coral reefs, loss of habitats. **Remedies:** less fossil fuel, solar and wind power, saving energy, public transport, planting trees, reducing and recycling waste.
- **As of 2026:** carbon dioxide in the air is above 420 parts per million, and the Earth is roughly 1.1 to 1.3 °C warmer than in the late 1800s. These figures rise with time; check the latest values from a recent source.
- The chemistry of these gases and their sources is dealt with in the ICSE Class 9 Chemistry chapter on the environment; here the emphasis is on the radiation and the energy changes.

sections.heading: 5. Energy degradation
sections.body_md:
When energy changes from one form to another, the **total energy is conserved**, but a part of it becomes **heat that spreads into the surroundings** and cannot be fully collected and used again. The energy is **degraded**: still present, but **less useful**.

- **Car engine:** chemical energy of the fuel becomes motion, but also heat and sound. Of 20000 J from the fuel, only 5000 J may become useful work; the other 15000 J is degraded.
- **Filament bulb:** most of the electrical energy becomes heat, only a little light.
- **Brakes, friction, a falling stone hitting the ground, rubbing the hands:** motion energy becomes heat that spreads out.
- Degraded energy = energy supplied − useful energy. Heat can be given in J or in cal (1 cal = 4.186 J).

key_terms.definition_md: The change of useful energy into heat spread through the surroundings, from which it cannot be fully recovered.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying "temperature is heat" or measuring heat in °C.
- Forgetting the factor 4.186 in conversions, or multiplying when you should divide (J to cal).
- Saying that water is lightest at 4 °C, or that a pond freezes from the bottom.
- Saying that greenhouse gases trap sunlight (they trap the infrared from the ground), or that the greenhouse effect is harmful in itself.
- Saying that energy is destroyed in a machine: it is only degraded.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions and differences (2 marks): heat and temperature, calorie, greenhouse effect, energy degradation.
- Graphs (2 to 3 marks): label the axes, and mark 4 °C as the peak (density) or the dip (volume).
- Hope's experiment (3 to 5 marks): apparatus, the two readings, and the reason in terms of density.
- Numericals (1 to 3 marks): formula, substitution and unit; show 1 cal = 4.186 J.

questions.solution_md: Natural and useful against extra gases from human activity raising the temperature.

marking_scheme.step: Greenhouse effect: natural warming by the gases
Global warming: rise caused by extra gases from human activities

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which the people of a city can lessen their contribution to global warming.

answer.model_answer_md: Use **public transport**, bicycles or walking instead of private cars, and **save electricity**; or **plant trees** and recycle waste. Each lowers the amount of greenhouse gas added to the air.

questions.solution_md: Any two: public transport, saving electricity, planting trees, recycling.

questions.stem_md: A car parked in the sun with its windows closed becomes much hotter inside than the air outside. Use the idea of the greenhouse effect to explain this.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sunlight** passes through the glass and **warms the seats and the dashboard**. These give out **infrared radiation**, which the **glass absorbs and does not let out** easily. So the energy is trapped and the air inside gets hotter, in the same way as in the atmosphere.

questions.solution_md: Sunlight enters; warm objects emit infrared; the glass traps it, so the inside heats up.

marking_scheme.step: Sunlight enters through the glass and warms the objects
The warm objects give out infrared that the glass does not let out
Trapped energy raises the temperature, as in the greenhouse effect

questions.stem_md: State three harmful effects of global warming on life on the Earth.

answer.model_answer_md: Any three: **melting of ice** and **rising sea level**, which floods coasts; **heat waves**; **droughts or floods** from changed rainfall; **damage to crops**; **bleaching of coral reefs**; loss of **habitats** of animals.

questions.solution_md: Any three: rising sea level, heat waves, droughts or floods, crop damage, coral bleaching, loss of habitat.

options.text_md: useful energy changes into heat that spreads out and cannot be fully used again
energy is destroyed in the machine
heat energy changes into more useful forms

questions.solution_md: Energy is conserved but the part that spreads into the surroundings as heat is less useful, option (a).

questions.stem_md: Most of the electrical energy given to a filament bulb is changed into
questions.solution_md: Only a small part becomes light; most is degraded to heat, option (b).

questions.stem_md: A stone falls from a height and stops when it hits the ground. The energy of its motion

options.text_md: is changed into heat and sound that spread out and are not recoverable
is stored in the ground as useful motion energy
is changed into an equal amount of useful energy

questions.solution_md: The motion energy is degraded to heat and sound, option (a).

questions.stem_md: A machine takes in 500 J of energy and does 150 J of useful work. Which statement about the other 350 J is correct?

options.text_md: It is destroyed, so the total becomes 150 J
It is stored in the machine as useful energy
It becomes useful work if the machine is run for longer
It is degraded as heat and sound in the surroundings, and the total energy is still 500 J

questions.solution_md: Energy is conserved, so 350 J has been degraded, option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The energy of the fuel burnt in a car engine is destroyed.

**Reason (R):** Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: (A) is false because the energy is degraded to heat in the surroundings, not destroyed; (R) is true, option (b).

questions.solution_md: Heat.

a greenhouse gas produced in paddy fields and by cattle

questions.solution_md: Anomalous expansion: contraction 0 to 4 °C; Hope: densest at 4 °C; methane: greenhouse gas; brakes: motion energy to heat; 1 kcal is 1000 cal.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by energy degradation? Give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: In energy degradation, **useful energy changes into heat that spreads into the surroundings** and cannot be fully used again, though the total energy stays the same. Example: the **heat and sound given out by a running car engine**.

questions.solution_md: Useful energy turns into spread-out heat; example: heat from an engine.

marking_scheme.step: Useful energy becomes heat spread out, not recoverable

questions.stem_md: A cyclist applies the brakes and the bicycle slows to a stop. Name the energy change that takes place and explain why this is an example of energy degradation.

answer.model_answer_md: The **energy of motion** (kinetic energy) of the bicycle is changed into **heat** at the brake pads and the rim. The heat **spreads into the air** and cannot be collected to set the cycle moving again, so the useful energy has been **degraded**, although the **total energy is conserved**.

questions.solution_md: Motion energy to heat; heat spreads into the air and cannot be recovered; total conserved.

marking_scheme.step: Heat spreads out and cannot be recovered

questions.stem_md: A machine takes in 8000 J of energy and gives out 2400 J as useful work. Find the energy that is degraded as heat and sound.
questions.solution_md: Degraded energy $= \text{energy supplied} - \text{useful energy} = 8000 - 2400 = 5600$ J.

questions.stem_md: A small engine takes in 12 000 J of energy, of which 30% becomes useful work. Find the energy that is degraded to heat, in calories. (1 cal = 4.186 J)
A lamp takes in 60 J of electrical energy every second and gives out 3 J of it as light. Find the percentage of the energy that is degraded to heat.
questions.solution_md: Heat $= 60 - 3 = 57$ J; percentage $= \dfrac{57}{60} \times 100 = 95$ %.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the apparatus used in Hope’s experiment, with its parts lettered A to E. A student notes the readings of the two thermometers every 10 minutes while the freezing mixture cools the water in the middle of the jar.

| Time (min) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upper thermometer (°C) | 10 | 10 | 9 | 4 | 0 |
| Lower thermometer (°C) | 10 | 6 | 4 | 4 | 4 |

(a) Name the parts A, B, C, D and E. [3]

(b) Which thermometer falls first, and what is its final reading? [2]

(c) Explain why the lower thermometer stops falling at this reading. [2]

(d) Explain why the upper thermometer reaches a lower reading than the lower thermometer in the end. [2]

(e) State the property of water that this experiment demonstrates. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is the tall glass jar; **B** is the freezing mixture (ice and salt) in the trough; **C** is the upper thermometer; **D** is the lower thermometer; **E** is the water.

**(b)** The **lower thermometer** falls first; its final reading is **4 °C**.

**(c)** Water cooled in the middle becomes denser and sinks to the bottom, and the **densest water collects at the bottom**; water at 4 °C is the densest, so the lower thermometer cannot fall below 4 °C.

**(d)** Water colder than 4 °C is **less dense**, so it **rises** and stays near the top; the top layer goes on cooling until it reaches **0 °C**, where ice starts to form.

**(e)** Water has its **maximum density at 4 °C**.

questions.solution_md: Jar, freezing mixture, upper thermometer, lower thermometer, water; lower, 4 °C; densest water at the bottom; colder water is lighter and rises; maximum density at 4 °C.

marking_scheme.step: Cooled water becomes denser and sinks
4 °C water is densest, so the reading stops
Water colder than 4 °C is less dense and rises

questions.stem_md:
The graph shows how the density of water changes with temperature from 0 °C to 10 °C. The vertical scale is stretched, so the changes look larger than they really are. The volume of 1 kg of water is 1000.16 cm³ at 0 °C, 1000.03 cm³ at the temperature of its greatest density, and 1000.3 cm³ at 10 °C.

(a) At what temperature is the density greatest? [1]

(b) State how the density changes (i) from 0 °C to this temperature and (ii) above it. [2]

(c) At what other temperature does water have the same density as at 2 °C? [1]

(d) Find the decrease in the volume of 1 kg of water when it is heated from 0 °C to the temperature in (a). [2]

(e) Find the increase in the volume of 1 kg of water when it is heated from that temperature to 10 °C. [2]

(f) Explain why the volume of a fixed mass of water is least when its density is greatest. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **4 °C**.

**(b)** **(i)** The density **increases**. **(ii)** The density **decreases**.

**(c)** **6 °C**.

**(d)** Decrease $= 1000.16 - 1000.03 = 0.13$ cm³.

**(e)** Increase $= 1000.3 - 1000.03 = 0.27$ cm³.

**(f)** Density is **mass divided by volume**; for a fixed mass, the smaller the volume, the greater the density.

questions.solution_md: 4 °C; rises then falls; 6 °C; 0.13 cm³; 0.27 cm³; density is inversely related to volume for a fixed mass.

marking_scheme.step: Mass fixed, so smaller volume gives greater density

questions.stem_md:
A heater gives 33488 J of heat to 500 g of water in an insulated vessel, so that no heat is lost. (1 cal = 4.186 J)

(a) Define the calorie. [2]

(b) Express the heat supplied in calories. [2]

(c) Find the rise in the temperature of the water. [3]

(d) A second vessel holds 100 g of water at the final temperature of the first vessel. State which vessel contains more heat, and what is the same for the two vessels. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** One calorie is the **heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C**.

**(b)** Heat $= \dfrac{33488}{4.186} = 8000$ cal.

**(c)** 1 cal warms 1 g by 1 °C, so the rise $= \dfrac{8000}{500 \times 1} = 16$ °C.

**(d)** The **first vessel** contains more heat, because it has **five times the mass** of water. The **temperature** is the same in the two vessels, so no heat flows between them if they are put in contact.

questions.solution_md: Heat to warm 1 g by 1 °C; 8000 cal; 16 °C; the first vessel holds more heat; same temperature.

marking_scheme.step: First vessel has more heat, with the reason of more mass

questions.stem_md:
In a cold country the water of a deep lake cools in winter until the surface freezes. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; of ice 900 kg m⁻³)

(a) Explain, using density, why the water at the bottom of the lake does not freeze, and state its temperature. [3]

(b) Why does the ice float, and how does the floating ice help the fish in the lake? [2]

(c) A closed metal tank is completely filled with 2000 cm³ of water, which then freezes. Find the volume of the ice formed. [3]

(d) Explain why the tank in (c) may crack. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** As the surface water cools it becomes **denser** and sinks until it is at **4 °C**, its greatest density. Water that is colder is **less dense**, so it stays above and freezes first. The water at the bottom therefore remains at about **4 °C**.

**(b)** Ice is **less dense** than water, so it floats. It is a poor conductor of heat, so it **shields the water below** from the cold air, and the water under it stays liquid for the fish.

**(c)** Mass of water $= 2000 \times 1 = 2000$ g, and the mass stays the same on freezing. Volume of ice $= \dfrac{2000}{0.9} = 2222.2$ cm³ (increase of 222.2 cm³).

**(d)** Ice occupies **more volume** than the water; in the **closed full tank** there is no room, so it pushes outwards with a large force and the tank cracks.

questions.solution_md: Densest water at 4 °C sinks, colder water rises and freezes; ice is less dense and shields the water below; 2222.2 cm³; ice needs more space in a closed tank.

marking_scheme.step: Cooled surface water becomes denser and sinks
Water colder than 4 °C is less dense and stays on top
No room in the closed tank, so it cracks

The figure shows the greenhouse effect, with its parts lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, B, C, D and E. [3]

(b) Explain how C helps to keep the Earth warm. [2]

(c) Name two gases that are present in C. [1]

(d) State two human activities that increase the amount of C in the atmosphere. [2]

(e) State two harmful effects of the resulting global warming. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is the Sun; **B** is the sunlight (visible light) reaching the Earth; **C** is the layer of greenhouse gases; **D** is the infrared radiation from the Earth’s surface; **E** is the infrared radiation that escapes into space.

**(b)** The gases in C **absorb part of the infrared** given out by the ground and **send some of it back** to the surface, so the surface stays warmer than it would otherwise be.

**(c)** Any two of: carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide.

**(d)** Any two of: burning coal, oil and petrol; cutting down forests; keeping large herds of cattle; dumping rubbish.

**(e)** Any two of: rise in sea level; heat waves; droughts or floods; damage to crops; bleaching of corals.

questions.solution_md: Sun, sunlight, greenhouse gases, infrared from the ground, infrared escaping; absorb and return infrared; carbon dioxide and methane; burning fuels and deforestation; sea level rise and heat waves.

marking_scheme.step: C absorbs infrared from the ground
Sends part of it back to the surface

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows how the 8000 J of energy taken in by a machine is shared. 2400 J becomes useful work, 800 J is lost as sound, and the rest, marked with a question mark, is lost as heat. (1 cal = 4.186 J)

(a) Find the energy lost as heat. [2]

(b) Find the total energy degraded, and express it in calories. [3]

(c) Find the percentage of the energy supplied that is degraded. [2]

(d) Explain why the degraded energy cannot be fully used again. [2]

(e) Is the total energy of the machine and its surroundings changed by the degradation? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Heat $= 8000 - 2400 - 800 = 4800$ J.

**(b)** Degraded energy $= 4800 + 800 = 5600$ J, which is $\dfrac{5600}{4.186} = 1337.8$ cal.

**(c)** Percentage $= \dfrac{5600}{8000} \times 100 = 70$ %.

**(d)** The heat and sound **spread out into the air and the surroundings** in all directions; it is **not possible to collect** them back to do useful work.

**(e)** **No**; the total energy is conserved, only part of it has become less useful.

questions.solution_md: 4800 J; 5600 J and 1337.8 cal; 70%; spread out in the surroundings and cannot be collected; no.
